cards.front: How is exercise order defined in resistance program design, and what is the primary objective guiding exercise sequencing decisions?
cards.back: Exercise order is the sequence of resistance exercises performed during one training session. Decisions are based on how one exercise affects the quality of effort or technique of another, ensuring an athlete's maximal force capabilities are available (via proper rest) to complete sets with proper form.

cards.front: What is the recommended primary sequence for ordering resistance exercises when power movements are included?
cards.back:
The primary recommended sequence is:
  • 1st: Power Exercises (e.g., snatch, hang clean, power clean, push jerk)
  • 2nd: Nonpower Core Exercises (e.g., back squat, bench press, deadlift)
  • 3rd: Assistance Exercises (e.g., biceps curl, triceps pushdown, lateral raise)

cards.tag: Rationale for Performing Power Exercises First
cards.front: Why must power exercises be performed first in a training session before other core and assistance exercises?
cards.back: Power exercises require the highest level of skill and concentration, involve extensive muscle recruitment, and cause high energy expenditure. Fatigued athletes are prone to poor technique and higher injury risk, so power lifts must be executed while athletes are metabolically and neurally fresh.

cards.front: What alternative terminology is commonly used in exercise science literature to describe the power → core → assistance ordering hierarchy?
cards.back:
Exercise science literature frequently refers to this hierarchy as:
  • Multijoint exercises performed before single-joint exercises
  • Large muscle areas trained before small muscle areas

cards.tag: Benefits of Alternating Upper and Lower Body Exercises
cards.front: What are the primary benefits of alternating upper body and lower body exercises during a training session?
cards.back:
Alternating body regions:
  • Allows one body region to rest while the opposing region works, maximizing recovery between body areas.
  • Decreases total session length by eliminating long rest waits between exercises.
  • Prevents excessive fatigue in untrained or beginner athletes.

cards.front: How can alternating upper and lower body exercises be modified to function as circuit training?
cards.back: When upper and lower body exercises are performed sequentially with short rest periods (20 to 30 seconds), the workout functions as circuit training, which can improve cardiorespiratory endurance (to a lesser extent than traditional aerobic training).

cards.front: How does alternating pushing and pulling exercises prevent premature muscular fatigue during a workout?
cards.back: Push–pull alternation ensures that the same muscle group is not stressed in consecutive exercises (e.g., bench press alternated with bent-over row). This prevents cumulative synergistic fatigue in prime movers and stabilization muscles like the triceps brachii or biceps brachii.

cards.front: How are common lower body resistance exercises categorized within a push–pull arrangement?
cards.back:
Lower body exercises are categorized as:
  • Lower Body Push: Leg press, back squat
  • Lower Body Pull: Stiff-leg deadlift, leg (knee) curl
(Note: Exercises like leg extensions have less clear push/pull classifications.)

cards.front: What defines a superset, and how does it utilize opposing muscle groups?
cards.back: A superset involves sequentially performing two exercises for opposing muscle groups (an agonist and its antagonist) with little to no rest between them (e.g., barbell biceps curl followed immediately by triceps pushdown).

cards.front: What defines a compound set, and how does its muscular strain differ from a superset?
cards.back: A compound set involves sequentially performing two different exercises for the same muscle group (e.g., barbell biceps curl followed immediately by dumbbell hammer curl) with little to no rest. Unlike a superset, it compounds fatigue on identical muscle fibers and motor unit pools.
